t: #2646 Minimize the Total Price of the Trips
o: Multiple trips run along unique tree paths; before them, we may halve prices on any set of nodes with no two adjacent, minimizing the total price paid over all trips. Since a node's saving depends only on how many trips cross it, first count cnt[u] = number of trips whose path contains u. Then it's a classic tree DP: choose halved/not-halved per node with the adjacency constraint. Example 1 halves {0,2,3} for a total of 23.
k: Trip paths are unique in a tree; find each path once (DFS parent walk) and tally cnt per node.
Tree DP with state (node, halved?) — a child may be halved only if its parent is not.
n ≤ 50 and ≤ 100 trips make brute-force path finding perfectly fine.

a.n: Approach 1: Path counting + tree DP over halving states
a.i: Root the tree at 0. For each trip, find the path via a DFS/BFS parent trace and increment cnt along it. Then dfs(u, parent) returns (costIfUHalved, costIfUNot): halved cost = cnt[u]·price[u]/2 plus children forced to 'not halved'; not-halved cost = cnt[u]·price[u] plus children at their cheaper option. Answer = min of the two root states. Prices are even, so halving is exact.
s: Build adjacency; write findPath(a,b) that marks parents via iterative DFS and walks back from b.
dfs(u,p): half = cnt[u]·price[u]/2 + Σ child.halfNotAllowed; full = cnt[u]·price[u] + Σ min(child states).
Return min over the root's two states.
a.t: O(T·n + n) — each trip costs O(n) to trace; the DP is linear

w: The decomposition 'aggregate demand, then independent-per-node optimization with an adjacency constraint' is the transferable idea. Pitfalls: trips with start == end (path of one node), integer division of prices (guaranteed even), and recursion depth on a path-shaped tree (small n keeps it safe; convert to iterative if worried). Follow-up: what if the graph had cycles (general independent set — NP-hard, so constraints matter).
